Would you take a shot from a bottle with a venomous pit viper staring right back at you? 🐍🥃

For generations of U.S. Marines stationed in Okinawa, Japan, taking a shot of Habu Sake—known locally as Habushu—has been one of the wildest rites of passage off base.

The Okinawan rice-based awamori liqueur is infused with a real habu pit viper coiled inside the glass. Producers age the snake in high-proof alcohol for months, which dissolves and neutralizes the venom before mixing the final bottle with honey and herbs.

Locals have long traded myths about its strength and energy, while service members still dare newcomers to take the first pour—even though customs rules make it tough to bring a bottle home.

Any Okinawa Marines in the comments—did you take a shot of Habu Sake, or did you pass? Drop your story below. 👇

“EVERYTHING YOU SAW ON CNN WITH MY FACE ON IT WAS A LIE. THEY DESTROYED MY LIFE.” — Retired SEAL Team 6 Operator Chris Beck Breaks His Silence on Detransitioning on The Shawn Ryan Show.

Former DEVGRU operator Chris Beck—who was celebrated globally in 2013 as the first openly transgender Navy SEAL—publicly renounced his transition on The Shawn Ryan Show (SRS #050), exposing how media networks and medical systems fast-tracked his transition while ignoring severe combat trauma.

In his own words:

“I had 20 years in the SEAL teams, 13 deployments, a Purple Heart, and a Bronze Star with Valor. When I retired, I was broken physically and mentally, full of severe TBI and trauma.

I walked into the VA, talked to a psychologist for less than an hour, and they handed me hormone pills. No real therapy, no digging into combat trauma—just immediate medical transition.

Within weeks, CNN and every major publication put me on prime-time television. They paraded me around as the face of the movement. I was used. I was naive, in a terribly vulnerable place, and they capitalized on my military credibility to push a political agenda onto American children.

It almost destroyed my life, my health, and my identity.

I am speaking out now to wake people up: I am not a woman. I am a man, a father, and a Navy SEAL. Everything they sold you using my face was propaganda.”

After 20 years in the elite special operations community and 13 combat deployments, Chris Beck is now speaking out to sound the alarm on medical gatekeeping, untreated veteran TBI, and media sensationalism.

What are your thoughts on Chris Beck’s warnings regarding the treatment of combat veterans dealing with severe brain trauma and psychological distress?

“AMBUSHED ON A 100-FOOT MOUNTAIN. HE SCALED THE VERTICAL ICE WALL UNDER MACHINE-GUN FIRE.” — The Heroism of Green Beret Matthew Williams.

On April 6, 2008, during Operation Commando Wrath in eastern Afghanistan’s jagged Shok Valley, Green Beret Operational Detachment Alpha 3336 (ODA 3336) and Afghan Commandos inserted into an insurgent stronghold perched atop a 100-foot near-vertical cliff.

As the lead assault force climbed the mountain, over 200 fortified fighters opened up from terraced caves and ridges with heavy machine guns, sniper fire, and RPGs—trapping the lead element on an exposed ledge with multiple critical casualties:

• Charging Through the Crossfire: Realizing his teammates were in danger of being overrun, Sergeant Matthew Williams gathered a team of commandos and charged across a 100-meter kill zone of ice-covered boulders and a freezing, waist-deep river under concentrated enemy fire.

• Scaling the 100-Foot Wall: Facing a near-vertical cliff of jagged ice and rock, Williams climbed straight up the mountain face while enemy rounds ricocheted off the rock inches from his hands to reach his besieged teammates.

• Evacuating the Wounded: When his team sergeant, Master Sgt. Scott Ford, was shot by sniper fire, Williams rendered field first aid under continuous fire, then helped lower Ford and other wounded soldiers down the sheer 100-foot drop to the casualty collection point.

• Climbing Back Up Into the Fight: Refusing to stay in safety, Williams scaled the cliff face a second time under relentless fire to defend the remaining isolated team members and recover four more critically wounded soldiers.

In six hours of brutal, high-altitude mountain combat, Williams repeatedly exposed himself to enemy fire to direct air strikes and guide in medevac helicopters. Every wounded American survived.

On October 30, 2019, President Donald Trump presented the Medal of Honor to Master Sergeant Matthew O. Williams, recognizing his extraordinary valor and refusal to leave his teammates on that mountain.

Scaling a 100-foot vertical cliff under machine-gun fire, lowering your wounded brothers down, and then climbing straight back up into the firefight—what does Matthew Williams’ courage tell you about the standard of America’s Special Forces?

MIZE, OLA L.

Rank and organization: Master Sergeant (then Sgt.), U.S. Army, Company K, 15th Infantry Regiment, 3d Infantry Division.
Place and date: Near Surang-ni, Korea, 10 to 11 June 1953.
Entered service at: Gadsden, Ala.
G.O. No.: 70, 24 September 1954.

Citation: M/Sgt. Mize, a member of Company K, distinguished himself by conspicuous gallantry and outstanding courage above and beyond the call of duty in action against the enemy. Company K was committed to the defense of "Outpost Harry", a strategically valuable position, when the enemy launched a heavy attack. Learning that a comrade on a friendly listening post had been wounded he moved through the intense barrage, accompanied by a medical aid man, and rescued the wounded soldier. On returning to the main position he established an effective defense system and inflicted heavy casualties against attacks from determined enemy assault forces which had penetrated into trenches within the outpost area. During his fearless actions he was blown down by artillery and grenade blasts 3 times but each time he dauntlessly returned to his position, tenaciously fighting and successfully repelling hostile attacks. When enemy onslaughts ceased, he took his few men and moved from bunker to bunker, firing through apertures and throwing grenades at the foe, neutralizing their positions. When an enemy soldier stepped out behind a comrade, prepared to fire, M/Sgt. Mize killed him, saving the life of his fellow soldier. After rejoining the platoon, moving from man to man, distributing ammunition, and shouting words of encouragement he observed a friendly machine gun position overrun. He immediately fought his way to the position, killing 10 of the enemy and dispersing the remainder. Fighting back to the command post, and finding several friendly wounded there, he took a position to protect them. Later, securing a radio, he directed friendly artillery fire upon the attacking enemy's routes of approach. At dawn he helped regroup for a counterattack which successfully drove the enemy from the outpost. M/Sgt. Mize's valorous conduct and unflinching courage reflect lasting glory upon himself and uphold the noble traditions of the military service.

“A STUDENT DROPPED A LIVE GRENADE IN THE PIT: THIS MARINE PUT HIS BODY IN FRONT OF THE BLAST.”

You have three seconds before a live fragmentation grenade detonates. On a live-fire training range at Camp Pendleton, a terrified student lost his grip. Staff Sergeant Brett Meil didn't hesitate—he shoved the young Marine behind him and placed his own torso directly in the line of the blast.

On June 13, 2023, then-Sergeant Brett D. Meil was serving as the position safety officer on the live-fire grenade range at the School of Infantry – West (SOI-West).

When a student inadvertently released the safety lever inside the throwing pit, activating the live M67 fuse, fear took over and the student froze. Recognizing the imminent explosion, Meil took immediate action:

Clearing the Pit: Meil forcibly wrestled the grenade away and threw both himself and the student out of the pit to escape the confined blast pressure.

The Fatal Ricochet: The grenade bounced off an interior bunker wall and rolled outside the pit, landing mere feet away on the dirt right next to the two Marines.

Becoming a Human Shield: With less than two seconds remaining, Meil grabbed the student, pulled the young Marine tight against his chest, and wrapped his entire body over him to absorb the blast.

Absorbing the Shrapnel: The grenade detonated, showering Meil with hundreds of high-velocity fragments. He took the brunt of the explosion across his back and limbs, saving the student, who walked away with only minor injuries.

Assessing His Marine First: Despite catastrophic wounds and intense bleeding, Meil’s first action was checking his student’s condition and calling for immediate medical support before allowing corpsmen to treat his own trauma.

On September 24, 2024, at Camp Pendleton, Colonel Patrick B. Byrne presented Staff Sergeant Brett D. Meil with the Navy and Marine Corps Medal—the Department of the Navy’s highest non-combat decoration for heroism.

“Staff Sgt. Meil performed exactly the way that we ask combat instructors to,” said Col. Byrne. “He identified that there was a dangerous situation, he assessed it and immediately acted exactly appropriately to address the danger and protect the student.”

For Meil, the instinct was immediate:

“My secondary thought was the grenade's outside the pit and pulling him as close and tight to me as possible.”

He was posthumously awarded the Navy Cross for his actions and valor during Operation Red Wings, in which he was killed. He served in that operation along with Michael Murphy, Daniel Dietz, and Marcus Luttrell. Dietz and Luttrell were also awarded the Navy Cross, the Purple Heart, and the Navy good conduct medals, where Murphy received the Medal of Honor.

Citation: For extraordinary heroism in actions against the enemy while serving in a four-man Special Reconnaissance element with SEAL Delivery Vehicle Team ONE, Naval Special Warfare Task unit, Afghanistan from 27 to 28 June 2005. Petty Officer Axelson demonstrated extraordinary heroism in the face of grave danger in the vicinity of Asadabad, Konar Province, Afghanistan. Operating in the middle of an enemy-controlled area, in extremely rugged terrain, his Special Reconnaissance element was tasked with locating a high-level Anti-Coalition Militia leader, in support of a follow-on direct action mission to disrupt enemy activity. On 28 June 2005, the element was spotted by Anti-Coalition Militia sympathizers, who immediately revealed their position to the militia fighters. As a result, the element directly encountered the enemy. Demonstrating exceptional resolve and fully understanding the gravity of the situation, Petty Officer Axelson's element bravely engaged the militia, who held both a numerical and positional advantage. The ensuing firefight resulted in numerous enemy personnel killed, with several of the Navy members suffering casualties. Ignoring his injuries and demonstrating exceptional composure, Petty Officer Axelson advised the teammate closest to him to escape while he provided cover fire. With total disregard for his own life and thinking only of his teammate's survival, he continued to attack the enemy, eliminating additional militia fighters, until he was mortally wounded by enemy fire. A champion of freedom, Petty Officer Axelson will be remembered for his self-sacrificing actions in the continuing Global War on Terrorism. By his undaunted courage, fortitude under fire, and unwavering dedication to duty, Petty Officer Axelson reflected great credit upon himself and upheld the highest traditions of the United States Naval Service. He gallantly gave his life for the cause of freedom.

The U.S. just test-fired an ICBM… one day before major nuclear talks. 

Late on November 17, an unarmed Minuteman III intercontinental ballistic missile launched from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California.

The missile has been in service for 56 years.
This was a routine operational test, the Air Force says — scheduled years in advance and not tied to any current events.

Still, the timing is hard to ignore.
The launch came just as high-level nuclear and diplomatic talks were about to begin.

Officials insist it’s pure coincidence.
Critics and observers are asking the obvious question:
Coincidence… or message?

These tests happen regularly to verify the reliability of the aging Minuteman III force.
But when they land this close to sensitive negotiations, people notice.

What do you think — scheduled routine, or deliberate signal?

Russia just flew nuclear-capable bombers past Japan… and landed them in Vietnam. 

On November 17, Japan reported that two suspected Russian aircraft briefly entered its airspace.
Fighters were scrambled.

Those aircraft turned out to be Tu-95 bombers — the same long-range, nuclear-capable platforms Russia has used for decades to probe defenses and send signals.

The bombers continued south and later landed in Da Nang, Vietnam.
A rare deployment that far from home.

Moscow is showing it can still project strategic aviation power deep into the Indo-Pacific, even while fighting a major war in Europe.
Japan sees it as a provocation.
Vietnam is hosting the aircraft without public comment so far.

For the United States, the question is straightforward:
Is this just routine muscle-flexing… or another reminder that Russia is actively working the Pacific theater while everyone’s attention is split?

Should America worry?

Kenneth Braun served as a Navy Corpsman alongside the Maines of India 3/9. At the Battle of Getlin’s Corner, the 19 year old Doc saved the lives of at least 35 Marines. He received the Navy Cross for his actions in 2005, 38 years after the battle.
⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
The unit came under heavy attack on the night of March 30, 1967. Marines fell everywhere as mortars, grenades, and machine gun fire rained down on their exposed position on the side of a hill. An NVA force more than five times the size of India Company moved into the attack. They shot Marine wounded in the head as they passed them. Ignoring painful shrapnel wounds, Doc Braun sprinted forward to every call of, “Corpsman up!”
⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
The company moved up the hill away from the NVA. Braun ignored orders to keep himself concealed in the elephant grass, and rushed back down over and over. He treated Marine after Marine and dragged them to safety. On multiple occasions, he encountered NVA in the grass, but managed to kill them first.
⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
Doc Braun located Lt John Bobo (Medal of Honor winner) as he single-handedly fought off the NVA in his area. Bobo’s leg was blown off below the knee. Braun cinched a web belt around the leg as a tourniquet and dragged Bobo up the hill. After 15 yards, they stopped to return fire. Braun stuffed the stump of Bobo’s leg into the ground to stunt the bleeding. An NVA soldier crept behind the Marines and let loose with his machine gun. Bobo was killed instantly. Doc Braun was hit three times in his back, exposing his spine. He managed to crawl up the hill to the Marines’ consolidated position. He coached his squad leader through patching up the holes in his back, and gave himself a shot of morphine. The squad leader later described Braun as “Superman,” having wounds that should have killed any man, and taking them without a single moan or sound of pain.
⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
While they waited for the next attack, a Huey gunship arrived and wreaked havoc on the NVA. Braun was evacuated to a hospital ship, and eventually medically retired due to his wounds. The Navy Cross he received in 2005 added to his Bronze Star with “V” and two Purple Hearts.

Sgt. Philip A. McCulloch, Jr.
3rd Battalion, 5th Marines
Sangin, Afghanistan, Jan. 2011
Award: Silver Star

During a six-hour engagement with insurgent forces in the Sangin District, Sgt. McCulloch led his squad of Marines in a determined pursuit of a numerically superior enemy force. After being attacked by enemy fighters, he personally led his squad's counter attack by assuming point and closing on the enemy, pausing just long enough to destroy an enemy fighting positions with an AT-4. Once he regained the initiative, he pursued the enemy into a nearby row of compounds and forced them into fixed positions where many of them were destroyed by close air support and indirect fires, combined with maneuver ... Throughout the engagement, he aggressively drove his Marines to remain focused, exposing himself to enemy fire to identify enemy positions and coordinate fires in support of maneuver. Even after beginning to return to base, as the enemy again engaged the Marines, he controlled another section of helicopters with devastating effects, allowing his squad to return to friendly lines." (U.S. Marine Corps photo by Lance Cpl. Eric Quintanilla)

He was the voice of Bambi.
Then he became a Marine… and never told his troops. 

As a little boy, Donnie Dunagan was the voice of young Bambi in the classic Disney film.
That soft, innocent voice millions of kids grew up hearing.

Years later he joined the Marine Corps.
He served three tours in Vietnam.
He earned a Bronze Star and three Purple Hearts.

And almost no one in his units knew about the Disney connection.
He kept it quiet.
No stories about the movie set. No “hey, I was Bambi.”
Just a Marine doing the job.

Maj. Donnie Dunagan passed away on November 4 at the age of 92.

From the voice of a cartoon deer to a combat Marine who earned three Purple Hearts…
and chose not to trade on the fame.

Some people live two completely different lives and somehow make both of them count.

Rest easy, Major.

Jennifer M. Moreno. Moreno was assigned to a U.S. Army Ranger unit in Afghanistan. On Oct. 5, 2013, she was killed in action during a patrol that would take the lives of two Army Rangers.

During a Special Operations raid in Zhari District (Afghanistan), when a suicide bomber initiated an ambush in the compound the army team was entering. During the twelve additional blasts that injured 30 Rangers and killed three, Moreno chose to not follow stand-by procedure in order to give essential medical assistance to a fellow soldier trapped nearby, which resulted in the triggering of another IED that led to her death at the age of 25. She was posthumously promoted to captain and awarded the Purple Heart, Combat Action Badge and Bronze Star.

Is Everyone Overreacting to the 2026 Midterms?You’ve probably seen the posts calling this election a historic disaster for Republicans.
But take a look at the actual House numbers:Bill Clinton lost 54 seats in 1994  
Barack Obama lost 63 seats in 2010  
Donald Trump just lost 41 seats in 2026

Forty-one is a clear loss. No question.
But it’s not the biggest midterm seat drop in recent decades. Presidents almost always lose seats in the House during midterms. That’s been the pattern for a long time.So when people treat 41 seats like the end of the world, it feels a bit overblown if you’re only looking at the House.That said, the full picture is more complicated.
Democrats also flipped the Senate and won some surprising races in traditionally red states. Those results matter and give the other side real momentum.Still, the pure House seat count that everyone’s screaming about isn’t as unprecedented as the reactions suggest.

After his first application to the Blue Angels was turned down, Donnie L. Cochran reapplied a year later and was selected in 1985 as the team's first Black pilot. In November 1994, he made history again by returning as the squadron's first Black commanding officer and #1 flight leader.

From Pelham, Georgia to Jet #1—drop a salute in the comments for Capt. Donnie Cochran.

Whitehall, London. Outside 10 Downing Street.

Two decorated alumni from The Shawn Ryan Show representing the very pinnacle of American and British Tier-1 Special Operations reunited in London:

On the Left: Former U.S. Army Delta Force (1st SFOD-D) operator Kyle Morgan—recipient of the Distinguished Service Cross for his heroic counter-assault during the 2015 Radisson Blu hotel terrorist siege in Bamako, Mali, and founder of Blu Bearing Solutions.

In the Center: A UK Metropolitan Police Authorised Firearms Officer (AFO) on armed counter-terror security duty outside the Prime Minister’s residence, carrying a SIG Sauer MCX platform.

On the Right: Former British 22 Special Air Service (22 SAS) operator Jay Cal (featured on SRS Episode #214)—veteran of both the Royal Marines and the SAS Regiment.

The bond between Delta Force and the 22 SAS is the closest brotherhood in modern military history.

In the late 1970s, Colonel Charles Beckwith served on exchange with the British 22 SAS in the jungles of Malaya. Inspired by their selection and counter-terror tactics, Beckwith returned to the U.S. and built Delta Force using the SAS model as its foundation.

From the streets of Baghdad during Task Force Black to covert joint target interdictions across the globe, Delta and the SAS have hunted together in the dark for decades.

"Who Dares Wins."

The three-star general in charge of Air Force training just made his No. 1 priority crystal clear — getting newly trained Airmen to be more like Marines.

Speaking at a Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies event Monday, Air Education and Training Command boss Lt. Gen. Clark Quinn said he wants to build a stronger Airman identity by having new recruits emulate the culture of the Marine Corps — while also rolling out iPads and AI-assisted study tools for Gen-Z trainees.

Can you really build Marine Corps culture inside the Air Force, or are the two branches just wired differently?

He fled Vietnam as a 4-year-old refugee.
Now he wants to run the entire U.S. Navy. 

Hung Cao’s story is the kind America used to celebrate without hesitation.

His family escaped Vietnam when he was just four years old.
He grew up, joined the Navy, became a captain, and later entered politics.
Today he is the Acting Secretary of the Navy — and he’s asking the Senate to confirm him permanently.

On November 17 he sat through a tough confirmation hearing.
Senators from both parties pressed him hard on readiness, long deployments, the strain of ongoing operations, and whether he has the right vision for the fleet.

Some see a classic American success story: a refugee who rose through the ranks and now stands ready to lead the world’s most powerful navy.
Others have serious questions about his recent performance as acting secretary and whether he needs more distance from active-duty service.

The Senate will decide soon.

A refugee who arrived with almost nothing is now one step away from becoming Secretary of the Navy.

Should the Senate confirm him?

“VIOLENT STORM OVERWHELMED VESSEL: AIR FORCE EOD JUMPMASTER SAVES DROWNING SURVIVORS AT SEA.”

When a violent ocean storm hit with mountainous swells, freezing temperatures, and treacherous rip currents, people were thrown into the open sea and within minutes of drowning. Senior Master Sergeant Joseph Riemer dove straight in.

An elite Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) flight leader and the first EOD technician in U.S. Air Force history to earn the Military Freefall Jumpmaster Badge, Riemer was at sea when disaster struck:

Hearing desperate cries for help, Riemer immediately plunged into the freezing, turbulent ocean, battling massive swells and rip currents to reach the scattered victims.

Reaching the survivors, Riemer used water survival techniques to keep them afloat, quickly assessing that two airmen had exhausted their strength and were moments away from slipping beneath the surface.

Fighting Back with Flotation Gear: Riemer fought his way back through the punishing waves to the boat, retrieved emergency life preservers, swam back into the violent sea, and secured the drowning victims in flotation vests.

 Swimming against powerful currents, he towed the victims through the swells to within 25 meters of the vessel, secured a heavy safety line, and hauled them safely aboard before ensuring everyone was accounted for on the return to port.

In March 2025, Brigadier General Brian Hartless presented Senior Master Sergeant Joseph Riemer with the Airman’s Medal—the Department of the Air Force's highest decoration for heroism outside of combat.

A combat veteran of Operations Enduring Freedom, Inherent Resolve, and Freedom's Sentinel, Riemer currently serves as the Senior Enlisted Leader for the Air Force Civil Engineer Center EOD Division at Tyndall Air Force Base, where he was also named the 2024 AFMC Outstanding EOD Master Blaster of the Year.

Trump just noticed the gas price drop… and questioned the timing.

Gas prices have fallen sharply.
According to AAA, the national average is now around $3.75 a gallon — down roughly 55 cents in the past month.

Trump’s response?
“Notice that they waited until after the ‘election?’”

He offered no evidence that the drop was deliberately delayed.
In reality, prices had already been trending downward in the weeks leading up to Election Day, driven by normal seasonal factors, higher production, and lower demand.

Still, the comment landed exactly as intended.
When prices are high, politicians get blamed.
When they fall, the same politicians often claim credit — or in this case, raise suspicions about the timing.

Whether you see it as a fair question or classic political deflection, one thing is clear:
Gas prices remain one of the most emotionally charged numbers in American politics.

What do you make of the timing claim?

Capt. Derek Herrera had vowed to leave the Marine Corps the same way he entered it: on his own feet. Aided by robotic leg braces, this Marine, paralyzed from the chest down by a sniper in Afghanistan, walked across a parade ground at Camp Pendleton to receive a Bronze Star for bravery. Herrera, 30, a Naval Academy graduate, is set to retire next week. He is studying for an MBA at UCLA and plans to become involved in helping veterans. "Your drive and determination are great, and you will continue to do great things," Lt. Col. John Lynch told Herrera. Some 300 Marines and other guests watched in respectful silence as Herrera, his wife Maura, and his service dog Shaggy arrived at the ceremony. The only sound was the soft whirring of the robotic system's motors. Herrera is the first person in the country to purchase a ReWalk system, according to the manufacturer, ReWalk Robotics Ltd.

The duct-taped American Airlines passenger just had his state charges dropped.

You remember the video.
A passenger completely wrapped in duct tape and zip ties, restrained in his seat after an alleged mid-flight meltdown.

On a September 3 American Airlines flight from Dallas to Newark, Arthur “Layne” Lundeen is accused of launching into racial slurs, anti-gay insults, and disruptive behavior toward the crew.
Fellow passengers eventually taped him down.
The flight was forced to divert to Baltimore.

Maryland had charged him with second-degree assault and disorderly conduct.

81 years after it was shut down, the name of America’s legendary WWII spy and commando agency is back at the Pentagon. 

The Office of Strategic Services.
The original OSS.
The unit that trained the first American special operators, ran daring missions behind enemy lines, and helped lay the foundation for both the CIA and modern special operations forces.

In a November 2 memo, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth directed that the Pentagon’s special operations civilian office take on the historic title: Office of Strategic Services.

It’s more than just a name change.
The move is part of an effort to elevate the role, give it more staff, more funding, and higher standing inside the Department of Defense — treating special operations more like a full military service.

Congress still has to make the biggest pieces permanent.

Some will see it as a powerful symbolic return to the roots of American unconventional warfare.
Others will call it mostly branding.

Either way, the name that once struck fear into Axis forces is back on official Pentagon paperwork for the first time in eight decades.

Big move… or just a name?

U.S. Army Lieutenant Colonel Kathryn Van Auken and Major Lauralee Flannery were awarded the Bronze Star with "V" for valor for their sustained courage and heroic performance of duties while serving in Operation Iraqi Freedom.

Van Auken and Flannery had been serving together in Iraq in support of a Kuwait Exploitation Team's objective to secure, safeguard, and assist a Kuwait forensic team in the recovery of the remains of Kuwaiti Prisoners of War and Missing from the end of the 1991 Gulf War. 

Van Auken and Flannery were traveling together in the lead vehicle on February 14, 2007. They had been tasked with escorting the Kuwait Forensic Team's convoy of 12 vehicles.

It was approximately 7:30 a.m. when the middle four vehicles of the convoy were hit with the largest planned improvised explosive device (IED) attack that had been recorded up until that time. 

Ten daisy-chained 155mm mortar rounds had been buried under the raised causeway they were traveling on south of Razzazah Lake in the vicinity of Karbala, Iraq. 

When these IEDs exploded, three vehicles were destroyed, and passengers -- disoriented and bleeding -- began exiting their vehicles. 

We both exited our vehicle," Van Auken said. "[MAJ Flannery] headed east and I headed west trying to gather up everyone and secure both ends of the roadway against secondary attacks."

As team leader, Van Auken deployed rapidly, undertaking a multiplicity of actions, quickly radioing instructions to move all vehicles through the smoke and debris and to follow her vehicle into safety away from the IED site to avoid secondary devices. 

In this highly fluid situation, vehicles became disabled. Van Auken and Flannery quickly ordered the destroyed vehicles to be pushed out of the kill zone by follow-on vehicles in the convoy in order to assemble the team and get everyone to a safe and secure distance. 

Van Auken then maneuvered the front column of Polish security elements and Korean Engineer vehicles into security postures along the west side of the raised causeway with great speed and determination gaining the advantage against any follow-on IED or possible ambush. 

Both soldiers reacted fearlessly and without hesitation, running alone down the west end of the roadway to halt any oncoming traffic, orienting Iraqi vehicles to block the road, dismissing large crowds gathering, and re-positioning Polish security forces to assist. 

The team provided medical assistance to their Kuwaiti team members who had been badly cut with glass and debris and who were vomiting and shaking on the side of the road from the shocking experience. 

Their actions provided an example of urgency and purpose to fellow coalition forces, and their courage under fire unquestionably saved the lives of coalition forces, particularly the civilians in their charge.

" We are battle buddies to the end," Van Auken said.

B-1 bomber pilots are now training in this little business jet…
and it’s giving them 100 extra flight hours a year. 

The B-1 Lancer is one of the most expensive aircraft in the Air Force inventory to fly.
Every hour in that bomber costs serious money — and those hours are limited.

So the Air Force came up with a workaround.

Near Dyess Air Force Base, B-1 pilots are now flying contractor-owned light jets (HondaJets) under a new program called BSTAR.
These smaller, much cheaper aircraft let them practice core flying skills — instrument work, handling, crew coordination — without burning through precious B-1 flight hours.

The result?
About 100 additional hours in the air each year for each participating pilot.

The expensive bomber hours stay focused on the things only a B-1 can do: aerial refueling, weapons employment, and combat tactics.

Some will say it’s a smart, cost-effective way to keep pilots sharp.
Others might wonder if training in a tiny business jet really prepares you for a 150-foot-long bomber.

Either way, the Air Force is betting that more time in the air — even in a smaller plane — is better than sitting on the ground.

Smart move?

The President of the United States of America, authorized by Act of Congress July 9, 1918, takes pleasure in presenting the Distinguished Service Cross to Sergeant Craig David Warfle, United States Army, for extraordinary heroism in connection with military operations against an armed enemy from August 18 to 19, 2010 during combat operations against an armed enemy of the United States as an Automatic Rifleman for a Joint Task Force in support of Operation Enduring Freedom. During this period, Specialist Warfle, with total disregard for his own personal safety, maneuvered on a fortified enemy machine gun position through effective enemy fire. Even after being wounded, Specialist Warfle continued to suppress the enemy with high volumes of effective fire in order to allow his team members to pull his unconscious element leader to safety. Specialist Warfle refused to be medically evacuated from the fight and his actions allowed the Platoon to hastily withdraw and defeat the enemy utilizing air assets. Specialist Warfle's distinctive accomplishments are in keeping with the finest traditions of military service and reflect great credit upon himself, this Command, and the United States Army. NARRATIVE TO ACCOMPANY AWARD: Specialist Craig D. Warfle distinguished himself by exceptionally valorous achievement as a Ranger Squad Automatic Weapons Gunner on August 18, 2010 while deployed to Afghanistan in support of Operation Enduring Freedom. Specialist Warfle was assigned to a task force, whose mission was to capture or kill Al Qaeda (AQ) and Taliban (TB) Senior Leadership. Specialist Warfle's valorous actions under effective fire while executing an objective saved the lives of his teammates and were instrumental in the death of at least 16 Taliban fighters, the removal of two Taliban Provincial Commanders, and the recovery of a large cache of weapons intended for use against Coalition Forces. On August 18, 2010, the team received special intelligence indicating that a Taliban Commander and weapons facilitator, was meeting near a tree line with at least 17 other Taliban fighters. Information gathered indicated that the enemy was orchestrating an ambush on Coalition Forces in Logar Province, Afghanistan. The team observed the fighters in position for the attack to include multiple spotters and runners used to communicate between the various fighting locations. The Battle Space Owner was notified of the imminent threat and diverted all convoys. When the enemy fighters aborted their attack they were observed walking in a military formation back towards a meeting site along a tree line. En route to that location the enemy fighters were positively identified to be carrying weapons. The team initiated a kinetic strike on the fighter's location from two AH-64s. The team stood ready and boarded two CH-47 helicopters for insertion once the kinetic strike was complete. Immediately after the kinetic strike, the team inserted a Ranger Element onto the hot landing zone to the West of the target area to eliminate the several remaining enemy combatants. Ranger Element 1, consisting of Specialist Warfle and five others, were tasked with isolating the Northern side of the tree line and suppressing the enemy to allow Ranger Element 2 to assault from West to East. Upon infiltration the Ranger Assault Force received effective enemy fire in vicinity of the North-South running tree line where the AH-64s had just completed gun runs. As soon as Specialist Warfle stepped off the ramp he came under fire from multiple enemy positions and without hesitation returned fire and crawled 15 meters through the muddy field towards the enemy. From this position, Specialist Warfle suppressed the multiple enemy positions with 150 rounds from his MK-46 allowing Ranger Element 1 to move to the North and Ranger Element 2 to maneuver to the South. Under fire and with no cover in the open field, Specialist Warfle continued to suppress the enemy positions permitting members of the Assault Force to get down in the prone position while the leaders determined a way to assault the enemy positions. After a couple of minutes passed, Ranger Element 2 came under heavy effective fire from enemy crew served weapons. Realizing that Ranger Element 2 was effectively pinned down in the open field to the South, Specialist Warfle moved with Sergeant Lugo to the North to flank the enemy position from the North-West. Specialist Warfle, while under heavy effective enemy fire, advanced on the enemy position to suppress the enemy and allow the Assault Force to maneuver on and destroy the entrenched enemy. As Sergeant Lugo and Specialist Warfle voluntarily maneuvered towards the enemy positions they identified two entrenched enemy personnel with automatic weapons firing on the Assault Force. Specialist Warfle continued to advance on the entrenched enemy using suppressive fire alone to protect Sergeant Lugo and himself because there was no available cover in open terrain. When Sergeant Lugo and Specialist Warfle got within 25 meters of the enemy machine gun positions, Specialist Warfle and Sergeant Lugo were both hit with a volley of machine gun fire. Although Specialist Warfle knew he had been shot in the right shoulder he disregarded his own personal safety and moved through the kill zone to Sergeant Lugo's side to protect his incapacitated Squad Leader. Specialist Warfle purposefully positioned himself in the line of enemy fire and immediately suppressed the enemy in order to defend Sergeant Lugo and provide covering fire for the platoon medic, Sergeant Solomon, to move to and treat Sergeant Lugo. Specialist Warfle fearlessly continued to provide accurate suppressive fire from his exposed position, allowing Staff Sergeant Myers and Sergeant Kochli the ability to move forward, suppress the enemy, and then subsequently evacuate Sergeant Lugo. Specialist Warfle continued to provide suppressive fire as Sergeant Solomon, Staff Sergeant Tucker, and Sergeant Kochli pulled Sergeant Lugo back to cover. Only after the casualty evacuation aircraft evacuated Sergeant Lugo, did Specialist Warfle treat the through and through gunshot wound to his right shoulder by applying a tourniquet to his right arm. Specialist Warfle then proceeded to engage the enemy position from a position between the enemy and the Platoon for over twenty minutes while the Assault Force reconsolidated and moved back away from the enemy positions. He steadfastly remained at his forward position delivering accurate fire on the enemy until all members of the Assault Force had moved across the open field to cover 100 meters to the West. Specialist Warfle bounded back to the West over the open field while the Assault Force provided suppressive fire. Specialist Warfle's actions allowed the Assault Force to break contact, drop ordnance on the enemy positions, and safely move to the exfiltration hot landing zone. By repeatedly risking his life for others, Specialist Warfle's purposeful gallant actions, selfless dedication to the safety of his teammates, and demonstrated extraordinary heroism were distinctive and exemplary. He is most deserving of the distinct recognition. Through his distinctive accomplishments, Specialist Warfle's personal actions reflect great credit upon himself, his unit, and the United States Army.
